e.t: This Hebrew noun means “house.” It normally refers to a dwelling or house and is used throughout the Old Testament in descriptions of places, possessions, giving, speech, and other actions connected with a house. It is a very common word, occurring 2,053 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Malachi. Its precise force in any verse depends on how the surrounding sentence uses the word.

“Bether” is a name used as a specific designation, rather than an ordinary descriptive word expressing an action, quality, or general object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Song 2:17, with the English rendering “Bether.” Since no short definition is available, the word’s precise identification depends on the surrounding passage and wider biblical context in this usage.

This Hebrew word means “proud” and describes a person marked by an elevated, self-exalting attitude. It functions as a descriptive word rather than naming an action or object. In the Old Testament, it is used eight times, appearing in Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its repeated association with people who stand above others gives the word a clear moral and relational force: it identifies pride as a recognizable posture toward God and other people.

In its five Old Testament occurrences, it is used for territorial boundaries in Joshua, Ezekiel, and Joel. The word can function as the object of statements about places being entered, reached, or situated, so it points to a defined boundary area rather than to a person or action.

There, it appears as something given, so the word identifies the liquid itself rather than the act of giving. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the verse’s instructions.

This Hebrew word refers to brightness or to the visible countenance, especially the appearance of a person’s face. In Daniel, it is used six times, all in six verses, and its rendering depends on whether the sentence emphasizes shining appearance or facial expression. Thus, it can describe outward brightness and also the look displayed on someone’s face. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea concerns visible appearance rather than an inner quality.

Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the geographic name Hermon.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Joshua.” It identifies the man who served as Moses’ assistant and later led Israel, rather than expressing a general action or quality. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, it occurs 218 times, especially throughout the book of Joshua. The name also appears in commands, speeches, and accounts involving Israel’s leadership, so its normal function is to name a particular person. The exact significance of the name in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Joiarib is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, rendered consistently as "Joiarib." The name occurs once in Ezra and four times in Nehemiah, in passages that identify people by name. Its specific significance as a personal name is not defined by the available lexical information; the surrounding verse is needed to explain the person’s role in each passage.

e.t: This word is the place name “Joppa,” a location mentioned in the Old Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than a description of an action, quality, or person. The Hebrew Bible uses it four times, in Joshua, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, and Jonah. These passages also connect Joppa with travel, arrival, and giving, showing its role as a significant place in the biblical narrative.

This Hebrew word functions as a predicate associated with “the,” helping identify or specify something in a sentence. It appears eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across passages in Kings, Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its exact force depends on the sentence in which it appears, but its ordinary role is connected with designation rather than describing an action or emotion. The word is especially associated with architectural descriptions in Kings and Ezekiel, as well as sayings and prophetic language elsewhere.

e.t: Jerah is a personal name. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it identifies a person listed in genealogical records, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears twice, in Genesis 10:26 and 1 Chronicles 1:20, and both occurrences are rendered “Jerah.” Its placement in birth and family-line records shows that it functions as an individual’s name within those genealogies.

This word is a Hebrew personal name, יָשֻׁבִי לֶחֶם, rather than a common noun or ordinary action word. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in 1 Chronicles 4:22. The available information identifies the name and its location but does not provide a separate lexical definition or enough surrounding verse text to explain its name meaning more precisely. Its role is therefore best understood as identifying a person in the genealogy or historical record where it appears.

In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears four times, naming Isaac in passages that also mention God’s covenant with Abraham’s family and the prophetic message concerning Israel. Its use remains specific to this person, so its meaning is best understood as the name Isaac, with the surrounding passage supplying the significance of each mention.

This Hebrew word means to “cover” or “covered,” describing something being placed over, hidden from view, or concealed. It can function as an action affecting objects, places, or what people can see. The word occurs 153 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its central idea is broad and recurring rather than limited to one setting. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being covered and the surrounding sentence.

This Hebrew word is an uncommon term whose precise meaning cannot be stated confidently from the available lexical information. It occurs three times in the Old Testament: twice in Ruth 1:13 and once in Job 30:24. Those references establish where it appears, but without an explicit definition or verse text, they do not safely establish what the word means. Its meaning must therefore be determined from the wording and surrounding context of each passage. Its normal sense is therefore a yoke as an instrument of restraint, service, or imposed weight; the surrounding verse determines which aspect is emphasized.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “foundations.” It refers to the foundational structures or established bases associated with something built or firmly set. In its Old Testament use, the word appears eleven times, including descriptions connected with the earth and with what is shaken or exposed. Its normal function is to identify the underlying foundation of something, whether viewed physically or as an established order. The precise force in any individual verse depends on that verse’s surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “habitations,” referring to places where people dwell. It functions as a noun naming dwelling places rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 49:5. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage cannot be described beyond this basic lexical sense. Its central idea is settled dwelling places.

This Hebrew word refers to something salted or treated with salt. Its clearest scriptural use points to the application or presence of salt, rather than to a broad spiritual idea supplied by the word itself. It occurs five times in the Old Testament, across four verses. Because no verse text is included here, its precise force in each occurrence depends on the surrounding passage, but the ordinary lexical sense is connected with being salted.

This Hebrew word expresses that something is “few” or states that it is or becomes so. It can describe a reduced amount, number, or extent, depending on the sentence. Rather than naming a particular object, it serves as the word that expresses this condition. It occurs 22 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing repeated use for describing limited quantity or degree. Its precise force in any passage depends on what the sentence says is few or how the state of being is expressed.

This Hebrew word describes movement or position “upward.” It points toward a higher place or direction and can function as a directional expression in a sentence. The word appears 140 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it has a broad normal use in descriptions of location, movement, or measurement. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea remains direction toward a higher point.

Its exact significance for a particular person comes from that passage’s surrounding context, but the word itself identifies someone named Eliezer.

It appears 26 times in the Old Testament, describing both the act of besieging and the defensive structures or conditions associated with it. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on how the surrounding sentence uses the word.

The word occurs 16 times in the Old Testament, appearing especially in Proverbs and also in historical and prophetic books. Its use identifies an individual within Israel’s recorded lineage, especially in priestly genealogy. Its meaning therefore centers on something marked off as distinctive, whether by a crown or by consecrated separation.

e.h: A Hebrew Word for a Fool
e.t: This Hebrew word means “fool,” identifying a person characterized by foolishness. It functions as a noun or descriptive name for someone viewed in that way, rather than naming a specific action. In the Old Testament, it occurs eight times, with most occurrences in Ecclesiastes and the remainder in Jeremiah. Its recorded uses connect the word with themes of speech and death, showing that foolishness can be recognized in both a person’s words and conduct.

This Hebrew verb means “stoned”: to kill someone by throwing stones at them. It describes the act of stoning rather than merely referring to an ordinary stone. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 22 times, especially in laws and narratives involving punishment. Its use as an action can be expressed in English as someone being stoned or as people stoning another person. The exact force in any verse depends on who performs the action and who receives it.

It is used when Scripture speaks about human beings in contrast with God, in questions about human weakness or worth, and in statements concerning human birth and survival. It occurs 42 times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, with especially frequent use in Job, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its exact force in any verse is clarified by the surrounding sentence.

e.t: This Hebrew word is rendered as “court” in Chronicles and “settle” in Ezekiel, so its ordinary sense depends on how it functions in the sentence. As “court,” it refers to a defined area associated with the temple. As “settle,” it functions verbally in descriptions of placement. The word occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across six verses, concentrated in 2 Chronicles and Ezekiel. Its uses are connected with temple courts and with giving or placing something in a specified location.

This Hebrew word refers to “Ummah,” a place name mentioned once in the Old Testament, in Joshua 19:30. It functions as a proper name rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. Because it appears only in this single reference and no verse text or broader lexical definition is available here, the safest understanding is simply the name Ummah. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding biblical context.

Amashai is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Nehemiah 11:13, and is rendered “Amashai.” Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide a separate definition, its ordinary significance is its role as a person’s name. The surrounding passage is needed to explain who this individual was or what he did there.

This Hebrew word means “branches,” referring to the limbs that extend from a tree. It is a noun describing part of a tree, especially its spreading growth. In the Old Testament, it occurs four times, all within three verses of Daniel 4, where the tree’s branches are described as extending outward and providing shelter. The word therefore points to the visible, spreading parts of a tree rather than to the tree as a whole.

Eran is a Hebrew personal name, referring to a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament and is rendered as “Eran.” The available record identifies its single occurrence in Numbers 26:36, but the surrounding verse text is not included here, so no further contextual meaning should be attached to the name. Its normal function is simply to identify the individual named Eran.

This Hebrew verb means “darkened.” It describes a condition in which something is no longer bright or clear. In its single Old Testament occurrence, it is rendered “darkened” in Isaiah 9:19. The word’s basic focus is the presence of darkness rather than a separate object, person, or action being named. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the subject connected with it.

This Hebrew word describes being “troubled”—an inward disturbance that unsettles a person. It is used when someone is deeply affected or unable to remain at ease, including reactions connected with dreams, thoughts, or powerful inner agitation. The word occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Genesis, Judges, Psalms, and Daniel. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a prostitute, a woman identified by her involvement in sexual relations for payment. It functions as a noun describing such a person, rather than an action or a general moral quality. The word occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in four verses, including passages in Genesis, Deuteronomy, and Hosea. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense consistently points to a prostitute.

This Hebrew verb means “winks,” describing an intentional movement of the eyes. It refers to communicating or signaling through a wink rather than through ordinary speech. The word occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Job, Psalms, and Proverbs. Its use in Proverbs connects this eye gesture with other actions that can communicate a person’s intentions. The precise force of the gesture in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears eight times in the Hebrew text, all within Daniel, and is associated with descriptions repeated in Daniel 2 and Daniel 7. Because no short definition, rendering, or surrounding verse text is available here, its narrower English meaning cannot be stated responsibly. Its use is therefore best understood by reading each occurrence within the sentence and vision where it appears.

The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both within Isaiah 24:16, so its recorded use is concentrated in one verse. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic lexical sense is the condition identified as “leanness.”

Its role is grammatical: it helps identify a particular noun in the sentence, while the surrounding noun and context supply the specific subject being identified. The word occurs in passages from Deuteronomy, Job, Psalms, Song of Solomon, and Habakkuk.

The word appears in passages naming or referring to individuals, while the surrounding text determines the particular person intended in each passage.

The word occurs 16 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, chiefly in descriptions of crafted objects. Its normal function is to identify this kind of connected structure rather than an action or quality.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a woman identified as the Shunammite, meaning someone associated with Shunem. It functions as a personal designation rather than describing an action or quality. The word appears eight times in the Old Testament, all in narratives recorded in 1 Kings and 2 Kings. Its occurrences concern the same kind of identifying designation, while the precise significance in any particular verse comes from that passage’s surrounding text.

This Hebrew word means “man.” It functions as a noun, identifying a person rather than naming an action or quality. The word occurs 13 times in the Old Testament, so it is an established term within that corpus rather than a rare isolated usage. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage. The available uses range across historical, poetic, and prophetic books, showing that the word appears in several kinds of Old Testament writing.

Shimshai is a personal name, rendered “Shimshai.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Ezra 4:8–23. The available references establish the name’s repeated use, but the verse text is needed to explain the person’s specific role in each passage. As a name, its meaning is best understood as identifying the same named individual wherever it appears in this section of Ezra.

This Hebrew word means “little,” marking something as limited in amount or extent. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 54:8. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s exact force in that sentence cannot be described beyond this basic sense. Its normal function is to indicate a small degree or amount rather than something extensive.

e.t: “Asher” is a Hebrew personal and tribal name in the Old Testament. It refers to Asher, the son of Jacob, and also to the Israelite tribe descended from him. The name appears in genealogical passages, tribal lists, and records concerning Israel’s tribes. It occurs 43 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Ezekiel. As a proper name, its exact reference—an individual, his descendants, or the tribe—comes from the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “longing,” expressing an intense inner desire for something. It functions as a term that describes what a person feels inwardly, rather than an outward action. In its only recorded Old Testament occurrence, it is rendered “longing” in Psalm 119:20. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on deeply felt desire. e.t: This word is the proper name “Togarmah.” It functions as a personal or group name rather than a general description or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears four times: in Genesis, 1 Chronicles, and twice in Ezekiel. Because it is consistently rendered “Togarmah,” its meaning is best understood as the named entity itself, while the surrounding verse determines what is being said about Togarmah in each occurrence.

This Hebrew word is a plural people-group name: “Asherites.” It refers to people identified by that group name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Judges 1:32. Because the word occurs only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its safest ordinary meaning remains the group designation itself. In a sentence, it functions as a name for a collective people.

e.t: Tikvah is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Tikvah.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus: once in 2 Kings 22:14 and once in Ezra 10:15. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its normal lexical function is as a person’s name. Both occurrences are represented by the rendering “Tikvah.”

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “crying,” naming an audible outpouring that can be heard by others. It is used four times in the Old Testament, in Job, Isaiah, and Zechariah, showing its use for a noticeable vocal sound rather than a silent feeling. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic idea is crying expressed aloud. The word appears in Job 36:29, Job 39:7, Isaiah 22:2, and Zechariah 4:7.
